page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Multiply by (1 − cosx)/(1 − cosx)
steps.why: Multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate (1−cosx) uses 1−cos²x=sin²x to turn the denominator into a single squared sine, which can then be split into two standard pieces.
common_mistakes: Multiplying by (1+cosx)/(1+cosx) instead, which reproduces the same denominator and gets nowhere.
Writing 1−cos²x as cos²x−1 with the sign flipped.
steps.memory_tip: Multiply by the CONJUGATE of the denominator's extra term — here (1−cosx), the opposite sign from (1+cosx).

steps.label: Split and integrate for the final answer
steps.why: ∫cosec²x dx = −cotx and ∫cosecx cotx dx = −cosecx are both standard derivatives, so subtracting the second integral flips its sign to give the +cosecx in the final answer.
common_mistakes: Sign slip on ∫cosecx cotx dx = −cosecx, forgetting the overall minus from subtracting this piece flips it back to +cosecx.
steps.memory_tip: ∫cosecx cotx dx = −cosecx; subtracting THIS integral flips its sign to +cosecx in the final line — two minus signs, easy to lose track of.
